title: Jobs, processes & signals
about: Foreground, background and suspended jobs; processes, PIDs and their parents; reading ps and top; signals, kill and exit statuses of killed programs.

questions.title: State of a job
questions.text: Where does each job stand in the shell right after the action described?

items.why: A plain command runs in the foreground: the shell waits and gives no prompt until it ends.

items.t: You run `fg` on a background job
items.why: `fg` brings the job to the foreground and the shell waits for it again.
The trailing `&` starts the job and returns the prompt at once.

items.t: You suspend a job with `Ctrl+Z` and then type `bg`
items.why: `bg` resumes the stopped job, but in the background.
The job is stopped (not ended) and stays in memory until you resume or kill it.

items.t: You run `kill -STOP %1` on a running job
items.why: `SIGSTOP` freezes the process just like `Ctrl+Z`.

questions.title: Effect of the ampersand
questions.text: What does putting `&` at the end of a command line do?

options.t: It starts the command in the background and returns the prompt at once.
options.why: The shell does not wait for the job; you can keep typing commands.

options.t: It runs the command with administrator privileges instead of those of your user.
options.why: Privilege has nothing to do with `&`; `sudo` does that.

options.t: It runs the command twice, once in the foreground and once in the background.
options.why: `&` does not duplicate anything.

options.t: It hides the output of the command by sending it to the null device.
options.why: Output still goes to the terminal unless you redirect it.

questions.title: Ctrl+Z is not kill
questions.text: After pressing `Ctrl+Z` on a running `sleep 100`, what is the state of that process?

options.t: Stopped: it still exists and can be resumed with `fg` or `bg`.
options.why: Suspending freezes it; nothing has terminated.

options.t: Terminated, and all of its memory and open files are released.
options.why: That is what `Ctrl+C` (or `kill`) would do.

options.t: Running in the background, exactly as if it had been started with `&`.
options.why: It does not run at all until you use `bg`.

options.t: Waiting for input from the keyboard, which it will read once you type.
options.why: It is frozen by a signal, not blocked on input.

questions.title: Job control commands
questions.text: Match each command with its effect.

pairs.r: List the jobs of the current shell
pairs.why: It shows numbered jobs with their state.

pairs.r: Resume a stopped job in the background
pairs.why: The job continues to run while you keep the prompt.

pairs.r: Bring a job to the foreground
pairs.why: The shell waits for it and it reads the keyboard.
`%n` refers to a job of this shell, not to a PID.

extras.r: Start a new shell for each job
extras.why: None of the commands above does this.

questions.title: Job numbers versus PIDs
questions.text: What is the difference between `%1` and a PID such as `4174`?

options.t: `%1` is a job number that only means something inside the current shell, while a PID identifies a process system-wide.
options.why: Jobs are the shell's own bookkeeping; the kernel knows only PIDs.

options.t: `%1` is the PID of the very first process that was ever started on the machine, which is always called `init`.
options.why: The first process is PID 1 (`init`/`systemd`) and is unrelated to job 1.

options.t: They are two different names for the same number, used in different commands.
options.why: They are independent numbering schemes.

options.t: `%1` is the name of a file in the current directory, expanded by the shell.
options.why: The percent sign introduces a job specification to `kill`, `fg` and `bg`.

questions.title: Resume in the foreground
questions.text: A job stopped with Ctrl+Z can be continued in the foreground with `{{0}}` and in the background with `{{1}}`.
questions.note: Both commands take an optional job spec (`fg %2`); without one they act on the most recent job, marked with `+` in `jobs`.

wrong.why: `jobs` only lists jobs; it does not resume any.

questions.title: Suspend and resume
questions.text: Put these steps in order for running a long command, pausing it and finishing it in the background.

items.why: The command must exist as a running job first.
This suspends it and returns the prompt.
This resumes the stopped job in the background.

items.t: Run `jobs` to confirm it is listed as Running
items.why: A check only makes sense after the state changed.

questions.title: Reading jobs output
questions.text: In the output of `jobs`, a line starts with `[2]+`. What does the `+` mean?

options.t: It marks the current job, the one `fg` or `bg` act on when no job number is given.
options.why: `-` marks the previous job.

options.t: It means the job is running with the privileges of the root user.
options.why: Users are not shown in `jobs`.

options.t: It means the job has already finished successfully and will be removed from the list the next time that `jobs` is run.
options.why: Finished jobs are reported as `Done`.

options.t: It means the job is using more than 100% of the processor time.
options.why: `jobs` does not report CPU usage.

questions.title: Jobs listing facts
questions.text: Select the true statements about the `jobs` command.

options.t: It shows only the jobs started from the current shell session.
options.why: Processes of other terminals are not listed.

options.t: `jobs -l` also shows the PID of each job
options.why: Plain `jobs` shows numbers and states only.

options.t: It reports the states Running, Stopped and Done.
options.why: That is the lifecycle of a job as the shell sees it.

options.t: It lists every process of the whole system
options.why: That is `ps -e`.

options.t: It is an external program in `/usr/bin`, like `ps`
options.why: It is a shell builtin because jobs belong to the shell.

questions.title: Closing the terminal
questions.text: You start `sleep 500 &` and then close the terminal window. What normally happens to the job?

options.t: The shell sends it `SIGHUP` when it exits, so it terminates unless it ignores that signal or was started with `nohup`.
options.why: The hangup signal was designed for "the terminal went away".

options.t: It keeps running forever, because a job that was started in the background is independent of the terminal that launched it.
options.why: Background jobs are still tied to the session.

options.t: It is moved to the foreground of the next terminal that you open on the same machine.
options.why: There is no such migration.

options.t: It turns into a zombie that can no longer be removed from the process table.
options.why: A zombie is a finished process whose parent has not collected it; that is not the case here.

questions.title: Foreground job and keyboard
questions.text: Which statement explains why only the foreground job can read what you type?

options.t: The terminal delivers keyboard input to the foreground job; a background job that tries to read it is stopped.
options.why: That is how the shell and the terminal share a single keyboard.

options.t: Background jobs are read-only processes and cannot use a keyboard at all, even briefly.
options.why: Only terminal input is restricted, and only when they try to read it.

options.t: The keyboard works only for the first job that was started in the terminal session.
options.why: Any job can be brought to the foreground.

options.t: The `&` operator disconnects the job from the machine, so that it cannot receive any input from the user at all.
options.why: It merely leaves the terminal to the shell.

questions.title: What is a process
questions.text: Which is the best definition of a process?

options.t: A program in execution, with its own PID, memory and open files.
options.why: The same program started twice gives two processes.

options.t: A file on disk that contains the machine code of a program and its data.
options.why: That is a program (an executable), not yet a process.

options.t: A command typed in the shell, together with its arguments and options.
options.why: A command line may start zero, one or several processes.

options.t: A user account, together with its home directory and its login shell.
options.why: Users own processes; they are not processes themselves.

questions.title: Identifying a process
questions.text: Every process has a unique numeric identifier called its `{{0}}`, and the PID of its creator is called its `{{1}}`.
questions.note: `$$` holds the PID of the current shell and `$PPID` that of its parent.

wrong.why: The UID identifies a *user*, not a process.

questions.title: The first process
questions.text: Which process is the ancestor of all other user-space processes on a Linux system and has PID 1?

options.t: `init`, today usually `systemd`
options.why: The kernel starts it last during boot, and it adopts orphaned processes.

options.t: `bash`, the shell of the first user who logs in
options.why: Your login shell is a descendant of PID 1, not the ancestor of everything.

options.t: `kernel`, which is listed as PID 1 in `ps`
options.why: The kernel itself is not listed as a normal process with PID 1.

options.t: `login`, which asks for the user name and password
options.why: `login` (or the display manager) is started by PID 1 later.

questions.title: How a command starts
questions.text: When you run `ls` from bash, what does the shell do at a high level?

options.t: It creates a child process that loads the `ls` program, and the shell waits for it.
options.why: The fork-then-exec pattern is how Unix starts programs.

options.t: It replaces itself with `ls`, so the shell disappears once the listing is done.
options.why: That is what `exec ls` does; normally you keep your shell.

options.t: It copies the `ls` code into its own memory and calls it like an ordinary function.
options.why: That is the behaviour of a builtin, not of an external program.

options.t: It asks the user to start `ls` in another terminal, and waits for the answer.
options.why: Nothing like that happens.

questions.title: Effect of exec
questions.text: What does `exec ls` do in a bash session?

options.t: It replaces the shell process with `ls`; when `ls` ends the session closes, as the shell no longer exists.
options.why: No new process is created; the same PID now runs `ls`.

options.t: It runs `ls` in the background and keeps the shell available at the prompt.
options.why: `exec` does not create a job.

options.t: It runs `ls` with administrator rights and then returns to the normal user.
options.why: `exec` does not change privileges.

options.t: It lists the processes that have been executed by the shell so far in this session, like the `history` command.
options.why: That is something `ps` or `history` would approximate.

questions.title: The three kinds of process
questions.text: Which are the usual categories of processes?

options.t: Interactive processes tied to a terminal, in the foreground or background.
options.why: What you start from your shell.

options.t: Batch processes that run scheduled or queued work, such as scripts run by `cron`.
options.why: No user needs to be present.

options.t: Daemons that work in the background providing system services.
options.why: Web servers, `cron` itself, `sshd`.

options.t: Only processes started by root.
options.why: Ordinary users own processes too.

options.t: Zombies as a fourth planned kind that are created on purpose.
options.why: A zombie is an error-like transient state, not a designed category.

questions.title: Kinds of process
questions.text: Match each example with its kind.

pairs.l: You run `find / -name x` in your terminal
pairs.why: You interact with it and can suspend or kill it from the shell.
Serves requests in the background from boot until shutdown.

pairs.l: A nightly backup script run by `cron`
pairs.why: Launched by a scheduler with no terminal.

extras.r: A service that keeps running in the background
extras.why: That describes none of the examples above; a finished process nobody has collected is a zombie, which is not a kind of daemon.

questions.title: Parent after death
questions.text: What happens to a running child when its parent process dies?

options.t: The child is adopted by PID 1 (or a sub-reaper) and keeps running.
options.why: Orphans are not killed automatically.

options.t: It is killed immediately by the kernel as soon as its parent has died.
options.why: That happens only with specific signals (like `SIGHUP` on hangup) or options.

options.t: It turns into a zombie at once, waiting for a parent that no longer exists.
options.why: A zombie is a *dead* child, not a live orphan.

options.t: It is moved to the foreground of the terminal where its parent was started.
options.why: Nothing is moved; the job table belonged to the parent shell.

questions.title: Zombie process
questions.text: What is a zombie process?

options.t: A process that has finished but whose entry stays in the process table until its parent reads its exit status.
options.why: It uses no CPU or memory beyond its table entry; it cannot be killed because it is already dead.

options.t: A process stuck in an infinite loop, using all the processor time it can get.
options.why: That process is running, typically state `R`, and can be killed.

options.t: A process that cannot be stopped even with `kill -9`, because it is waiting for the disk to finish an input or output request.
options.why: That describes uninterruptible sleep (state `D`), not a zombie.

options.t: A background process with no controlling terminal, such as a server started at boot.
options.why: That is a daemon.

questions.title: Killing a zombie
questions.text: Why does `kill -9` on a zombie not make it disappear?

options.t: It is already dead; only its parent reading the exit status (or the parent exiting) removes the entry.
options.why: There is nothing left to signal.

options.t: `SIGKILL` is blocked for every process whose state in `ps` is `Z`, by a kernel rule.
options.why: The process no longer runs, so signals have no effect at all.

options.t: Zombies are immune to signals because they always run with root privileges.
options.why: Privilege is irrelevant.

options.t: `kill -9` only works on background processes, while zombies are always treated as foreground processes by the shell.
options.why: It works on any process that can receive signals.

questions.title: PID size
questions.text: Historically PIDs were limited to 32767 for compatibility with 16-bit systems. What happens when the PID counter reaches the limit?

options.t: Allocation wraps around and reuses numbers that are not in use by live processes.
options.why: PIDs are recycled, so a PID is unique only among currently existing processes.

options.t: The system refuses to start any new process until some existing process has ended.
options.why: It would be unusable after a short time.

options.t: The machine reboots so that the PID counter can start again from the beginning.
options.why: Nothing so dramatic.

options.t: New processes receive negative PIDs, counting downwards from the limit.
options.why: PIDs are always positive integers.

questions.title: Variables about processes
questions.text: Select the special shell variables that hold process information.

options.why: PID of the current shell.

options.t: `$PPID`
options.why: PID of the parent of the current shell.
PID of the most recently started background job.
That is an exit status, not a PID.
That is the number of positional parameters.

questions.title: Subshell and cd
questions.text: Why does `(cd /tmp; pwd); pwd` end in the original directory?

options.t: The parentheses run the commands in a child shell, whose `cd` does not affect the parent.
options.why: Each process has its own working directory.

options.t: Because `pwd` always prints the home directory of the user when it runs inside a pair of parentheses.
options.why: It prints the current directory of the process that runs it.

options.t: Because `cd` does not work at all when it is placed inside parentheses.
options.why: It works, but only for the child.

options.t: Because the semicolon restores the previous directory after each command.
options.why: The semicolon only separates commands.

questions.title: Default ps output
questions.text: What does plain `ps` (no options) show in a terminal?

options.t: Only the processes of your current terminal, with the columns PID, TTY, TIME and CMD.
options.why: It is a short, per-terminal listing.

options.t: Every process running on the machine, for all users, in a long format.
options.why: That needs `-e` or `aux`.

options.t: Only the processes that belong to the user root, which is the owner of the system.
options.why: `ps` does not filter by root.

options.t: The jobs of the current shell, numbered from `[1]` with their states.
options.why: Jobs are shown by `jobs`.

questions.title: ps options
questions.text: Match each command with the listing it gives.

pairs.why: The most basic and shortest listing.
`-e` is "everything".
Adds fields such as UID, PPID, priority.

pairs.r: All processes with the owning user
pairs.why: BSD style; includes %CPU, %MEM and STAT.

extras.r: Processes sorted by memory and refreshed live

questions.title: Columns of ps aux
questions.text: Select the columns that appear in `ps aux`.

options.t: USER
options.why: The owner of the process.

options.t: %CPU
options.why: Share of processor time used.

options.t: STAT
options.why: The process state code.

options.t: COMMAND
options.why: The command line that started it.

options.t: UID only, never the user name
options.why: `ps aux` shows the name; `ps -l` shows the numeric UID.

options.t: JOBNUM
options.why: Job numbers belong to the shell, not to `ps`.

questions.title: Process state letters
questions.text: Match each STAT letter of `ps` with its meaning.

pairs.why: Using the CPU or ready to.
Interruptible sleep: for input, a timer, etc.

pairs.r: Stopped by a signal (for example Ctrl+Z)
pairs.why: Not running until continued.

pairs.r: Uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting for disk I/O
pairs.why: It ignores signals until the I/O ends.
Waiting for the parent to read its status.

extras.r: Terminated and removed from the table
extras.why: A removed process no longer appears in `ps`.

questions.title: T is not terminating
questions.text: In the output of `ps`, a process has state `T`. What does it mean?

options.t: It is stopped, for example suspended with `Ctrl+Z`.
options.why: `T` means stopped (or traced by a debugger).

options.t: It is terminating and will disappear in a moment.
options.why: Terminating processes are briefly in state `Z` or vanish; `T` does not mean that.

options.t: It is a system thread.
options.why: Threads appear with other markers, such as `l`.

options.t: It is waiting for a terminal.
options.why: That is normally state `S`.

questions.title: Trailing plus in STAT
questions.text: A `+` after the state letter, as in `S+`, tells you that...

options.t: the process is in the foreground process group of its terminal
options.why: Useful to see which jobs currently own the keyboard.

options.t: the process is using more processor time than the average process
options.why: STAT flags do not measure CPU.

options.t: the process has been given a higher scheduling priority than normal
options.why: That is the `<` flag.

options.t: the process is multi-threaded, with more than one thread of execution
options.why: That is the `l` flag.

questions.title: Find a specific PID
questions.text: To list all processes with a full view and filter those of the program `sshd`: `ps {{0}} | grep sshd`
questions.note: `ps aux` or `ps -ef` produces the full list; `grep` then filters it. (`pgrep sshd` is a shorter way.)

wrong.why: `jobs` is a shell builtin about jobs; it cannot be used as an argument of `ps`.

questions.title: top basics
questions.text: Which statement describes `top` correctly?

options.t: It shows a live, periodically refreshed list of processes, by default ordered by CPU use.
options.why: Updating the screen is its main difference from `ps`.

options.t: It prints the list of processes once and then exits, exactly like `ps` does.
options.why: `top` keeps running until you press `q`.

options.t: It lists only the processes that were started from your current shell session.
options.why: It shows the whole system.

options.t: It automatically kills the process that is using the most memory on the system, to keep the machine responsive.
options.why: It only displays; killing needs a key (`k`) or a command.

questions.title: Interactive top keys
questions.text: Which keys work inside the standard `top`?

options.t: `q` to quit.
options.why: Leaves `top` and returns to the shell.

options.t: `h` to show help.
options.why: Lists the available interactive commands.

options.t: `M` to sort by memory.
options.why: Changes the sort column from CPU to memory.

options.t: `k` to send a signal to a process.
options.why: Prompts for a PID and a signal.

options.t: `Ctrl+Z` to go back to the previous screen.
options.why: It suspends `top` like any foreground program.

questions.title: pstree
questions.text: What does `pstree` show that `ps aux` does not show at a glance?

options.t: The parent-child relationships between processes, drawn as a tree.
options.why: Good for seeing where a process came from.

options.t: The amount of memory used by each process, in a column next to its name.
options.why: Not its purpose.

options.t: The users that are currently connected to the system and their terminals.
options.why: That is `who` or `w`.

options.t: The history of the commands that each process has executed since it started.
options.why: That is `history`.

questions.title: pgrep
questions.text: Which command prints the PIDs of processes whose name matches `sshd`, without using a pipe?

options.t: `pgrep sshd`
options.why: It searches the process table by name and prints matching PIDs.

options.t: `grep sshd`
options.why: It would wait for input on standard input instead of searching processes.

options.t: `kill sshd`
options.why: `kill` needs a PID or job spec, not a name.

options.t: `jobs sshd`
options.why: `jobs` knows only your shell's jobs.

questions.title: Find and stop a runaway
questions.text: You notice a program eating CPU. Put the sensible sequence of steps in order.

items.t: Run `top` or `ps aux` to find the offender and its PID
items.why: You need the PID before you can signal anything.
Give the program the chance to clean up and exit.

items.t: Check with `ps -p PID` that it is gone
items.why: Verify the result of the first attempt.

items.t: Only if it is still there, send `kill -9 PID`
items.why: SIGKILL is the last resort because it allows no cleanup.

questions.title: What is a signal
questions.text: What is a signal in Unix?

options.t: A short notification sent asynchronously to a process to tell it that an event happened.
options.why: The process can react with a default action or its own handler, for most signals.

options.t: A message that one user sends to another user's terminal, like the `write` command.
options.why: That would be `write` or `mail`.

options.t: A special kind of file in `/dev` through which programs can talk to each other.
options.why: Signals are not files.

options.t: A shell variable holding the exit code of the last command that finished.
options.why: That is `$?`.

questions.title: kill is misnamed
questions.text: What does the command `kill PID` do by default?

options.t: It sends `SIGTERM` (15), a polite request to terminate that the program may handle or ignore.
options.why: The name suggests more violence than the default deserves.

options.t: It sends `SIGKILL` (9), which ends the process at once and cannot be caught.
options.why: That requires `-9` explicitly.

options.t: It erases the program file of the process from the disk, as well as ending the process that is running it.
options.why: Killing a process does not touch files.

options.t: It pauses the process until it receives a continue signal from the shell.
options.why: Pausing is `SIGSTOP`/`SIGTSTP`.

questions.title: Signal numbers
questions.text: Match each signal with its usual number on Linux.

pairs.why: The hangup signal.
What `Ctrl+C` sends.
The one that cannot be caught.
The default of `kill`.
The one that cannot be caught and freezes the process.

extras.why: There is no ordinary signal with that number; the standard ones stop below 32.

questions.title: Keys and signals
questions.text: Match each keyboard combination with the signal the terminal sends.

pairs.why: Asks the foreground job to interrupt.
Stop from the terminal (can be caught).
Quit and usually produce a core dump.

extras.why: No keyboard shortcut is bound to it by default.

questions.title: Uncatchable signals
questions.text: Which signals can a process **not** catch, block or ignore?

options.t: `SIGKILL`
options.why: The kernel always terminates the process.

options.t: `SIGSTOP`
options.why: The kernel always stops it.

options.t: `SIGTERM`
options.why: A handler can do cleanup before exiting.

options.t: `SIGINT`
options.why: Programs often catch it to ask "really quit?".

options.t: `SIGHUP`
options.why: Daemons often catch it to reload their configuration.

questions.title: Why not always -9
questions.text: Why is `kill -9` considered a last resort?

options.t: The process cannot run its cleanup code, so temporary files, locks or half-written data may be left behind.
options.why: `SIGTERM` lets the program close files and exit properly.

options.t: Because it requires the root password to be typed, even when the process to be ended belongs to the user who sends it.
options.why: It works on your own processes without any password.

options.t: Because it only pauses the process and does not really end it in any way.
options.why: It terminates it.

options.t: Because it makes the PID of the process unusable for the rest of the session.
options.why: The PID is freed and can be reused.

questions.title: Kill job number one
questions.text: To send SIGTERM to the first job of the shell, not to a PID: `kill {{0}}`
questions.note: The `%` marks a job specification, which bash resolves to the job's process group.

wrong.why: That would be PID 1, the init process. Normal users have no permission to kill it, and root should not.

questions.title: List the signals
questions.text: To print all signal names and their numbers: `kill {{0}}`

wrong.why: `-a` is not the option for that in bash.

questions.title: Signal names
questions.text: Which of these commands sends exactly the same signal?

options.t: `kill -9 123`, `kill -KILL 123` and `kill -SIGKILL 123`
options.why: Number, short name and long name are interchangeable in bash's `kill`.

options.t: `kill -9 123` and `kill -15 123`, since both end the process in the end
options.why: Different signals with different behaviour.

options.t: `kill 123` and `kill -9 123`, because 9 is the default signal
options.why: The first is SIGTERM, the second SIGKILL.

options.t: `kill -1 123` and `kill -2 123`, which differ only in their number
options.why: `SIGHUP` and `SIGINT`, two different signals.

questions.title: Killing by name
questions.text: Which command sends SIGTERM to every process whose command name is exactly `firefox`?

options.t: `killall firefox`
options.why: It selects processes by exact name.

options.t: `kill firefox`
options.why: `kill` accepts PIDs or job specs, not program names.

options.t: `jobs -k firefox`
options.why: No such option.

options.t: `ps firefox`
options.why: `ps` only lists; it does not send signals.

questions.title: Permission to kill
questions.text: Which processes may an ordinary (non-root) user send signals to?

options.t: Only processes owned by the same user.
options.why: Root may signal any process.

options.t: Any process of the system.
options.why: That would let anyone stop system services.

options.t: Only processes started from the current terminal.
options.why: Ownership matters, not the terminal.

options.t: None, `kill` is reserved for root.
options.why: Users normally manage their own processes.

questions.title: Exit status of killed process
questions.text: A foreground program is killed by `SIGKILL`. What does `$?` usually show afterwards in bash?

options.t: `137`, which is 128 plus 9, the number of `SIGKILL`
options.why: Bash reports death by signal N as 128 + N.

options.t: `9`, which is simply the number of the signal that killed the program
options.why: The signal number itself is not used as the status.

options.t: `0`, because a program that has been killed is counted as finished without an error
options.why: Success would be misleading for a killed process.

options.t: `1`, the general failure code that every killed program returns to the shell
options.why: That is a generic failure code, not a signal report.

questions.title: Killed-by-signal statuses
questions.text: Match each cause of death with the status bash reports.

extras.why: This would be the signal number; bash adds 128 for death by signal.

questions.title: SIGHUP on daemons
questions.text: Many daemons re-read their configuration file when they receive `SIGHUP`. What does that allow an administrator to do?

options.t: Apply new settings without restarting the service and without dropping it from the system.
options.why: A common convention: `kill -HUP PID`.

options.t: Restart the whole machine so that every service reads its configuration again.
options.why: Nothing reboots.

options.t: Delete the logs of the daemon so that it starts writing new entries from scratch, with an empty file.
options.why: Logs are untouched.

options.t: Change the owner of the daemon so that it runs as a different user afterwards.
options.why: Ownership is a file-system matter.

questions.title: Continue a stopped process
questions.text: A process was frozen with `kill -STOP PID`. Which command lets it continue?

options.t: `kill -CONT PID`
options.why: `SIGCONT` resumes a stopped process.

options.t: `kill -TERM PID`
options.why: It would ask the process to end.

options.t: `kill -HUP PID`
options.why: Hangup does not resume a stopped process.

options.t: `kill -STOP PID` again
options.why: It stays stopped.

questions.title: Sleep state after signal
questions.text: After `kill -STOP` on a `sleep 50` process, `ps -o stat= -p PID` prints `T`. After `kill -CONT` it prints...

options.why: It goes back to sleeping, waiting for the timer to elapse.
It is not dead.
That is the stopped state it just left.
That state is for uninterruptible I/O waits.

questions.title: Reasons a process ends
questions.text: Which events can end a process?

options.t: It finishes its work and returns an exit status.
options.why: The normal way.

options.t: It receives a signal it does not handle, such as `SIGTERM`.
options.why: The default action terminates.

options.t: It calls `exit()` after an error.
options.why: A non-zero status signals the failure.

options.t: You press `Ctrl+Z`.
options.why: That only suspends it.

options.t: You run `bg` on it.
options.why: That resumes it in the background.

groups.title: Trace: what do these commands do

questions.title: Trace 1
questions.text: What happens with `sleep 100 & kill $!`?

options.t: A background `sleep` starts and is then sent SIGTERM via the PID in `$!`, so it ends.
options.why: `$!` expands to the PID of the job just started.

options.t: `sleep` is killed before it starts, because `kill` runs before the background job.
options.why: It is already running by the time `kill` executes.

options.t: The shell itself is killed, since `$!` expands to the PID of the current shell.
options.why: `$!` is the background job's PID, not the shell's (`$$`).

options.t: Nothing happens, since `&` and `kill` cannot be combined in a single command line.
options.why: They can; separators like `;` or a newline are implied here by `&`.

questions.title: Trace 2
questions.text: After `sleep 100`, `Ctrl+Z`, `bg`, what does `jobs` list?

options.t: `[1]+  Running  sleep 100 &`
options.why: `bg` resumes it in the background, so it shows Running.

options.t: `[1]+  Stopped  sleep 100`
options.why: That was the state *before* `bg`.

options.t: `[1]+  Done  sleep 100`
options.why: It has 100 seconds to run.

options.t: Nothing, because `bg` kills stopped jobs.
options.why: `bg` resumes; it does not kill.

questions.title: Trace 3
questions.text: You type `sleep 60`, press `Ctrl+C`, and then run `echo $?`. What prints?

options.why: Killed by SIGINT (signal 2): 128 + 2.
A process killed by a signal did not exit successfully.
The argument of `sleep` is not its status.
Bash adds 128 to the signal number.

questions.title: Trace 4
questions.text: `sleep 100 & echo $!; echo $$` prints two different numbers. Which is which?

options.t: The first is the PID of the background `sleep`; the second is the PID of the shell itself.
options.why: `$!` is the last background PID; `$$` is the shell.

options.t: They are the same process seen twice, once as a child and once as a parent.
options.why: A process and its child have distinct PIDs.

options.t: The first is the PPID of the shell and the second is the exit status of the `sleep` job, which is still running.
options.why: Neither variable holds those.

options.t: The first is the job number of `sleep` and the second is its PID.
options.why: Job numbers are shown as `[1]`, never by `$!`.

questions.title: Kill the most recent background job
questions.text: Start a sleeper and end it right away: `sleep 300 & kill {{0}}`
questions.note: `$!` is the PID of the latest background command.

wrong.why: That is the PID of the shell itself; you would send SIGTERM to your own shell (which ignores it when interactive, but in a script it would end the script).
That is an exit status, which is almost certainly not the PID you want.

questions.title: Who runs what
questions.text: After `sleep 100 &`, `ps -o pid,ppid,comm` shows two lines. Which relationship do you expect?

options.t: The PPID of `sleep` equals the PID of `bash`.
options.why: The shell created the `sleep` child.

options.t: The PID of `sleep` equals the PID of `bash`.
options.why: Every process has a distinct PID.

options.t: The PPID of `sleep` is 0.
options.why: PPID 0 is the kernel's scheduler, not a normal parent.

options.t: The PPID of `bash` equals the PID of `sleep`.
options.why: The parent is the shell, never the other way round.

questions.title: Suspend and resume keys
questions.text: Press `{{0}}` to suspend the foreground job and type `{{1}}` to let it continue in the background.
questions.note: `jobs` lists the result; `fg` brings it back to the front.

wrong.why: That interrupts (normally ends) the job instead of suspending it.
That brings the job to the foreground, not the background.

questions.title: Send a signal by number
questions.text: Force the process with PID 4242 to end at once, with signal number 9: `kill {{0}} 4242`
questions.note: Try plain `kill 4242` first; it gives the program the chance to clean up.

wrong.why: That is `SIGTERM`, which the process may handle or ignore.

questions.title: Who catches it
questions.text: Classify each signal.

items.why: Programs may handle `Ctrl+C`.
The polite termination request.
Often used to reload configuration.
The kernel ends the process directly.
The kernel freezes the process directly.

questions.title: What ps shows
questions.text: Select the statements that are true about the output of `ps aux`.

options.t: Every process of the system is listed, not only those of your terminal.
options.why: The `a` and `x` options add other users' processes and those without a terminal.

options.t: The second column is the PID.
options.why: The first is the user.

options.t: A `?` in the TTY column means the process has no controlling terminal.
options.why: Typical for daemons.

options.t: Each line starts with the job number of the shell.
options.why: Job numbers belong to `jobs`.

options.t: Only root-owned processes are shown.
options.why: All users are shown.

questions.title: Tracing a hung program
questions.text: A program seems stuck. Put these steps in a sensible order.

items.t: Check whether it still exists with `ps -p PID`
items.why: Confirm it is the process you think it is.

items.t: Look at its state in the `STAT` column
items.why: `D` or `T` tell you very different things.

items.t: Send `SIGTERM` with `kill PID` and wait a little
items.why: Give it the chance to clean up.

items.t: If it is still alive, send `SIGKILL` with `kill -9 PID`
items.why: The forced last resort.

questions.title: Commands and what they change
questions.text: Match each command with the effect on a running job.

pairs.why: The job stays in memory.
The job runs again.
Same as plain `kill %1`.

pairs.r: Ends job 1 without any chance to clean up
pairs.why: Same as `kill -9 %1`.
